children: China’s taxman could become an unlikely engine of economic growth. A record $24 bln haul from offshore trusts in a single month suggests the People's Republic could garner more revenue from widening levies and tougher enforcement. The state could use that extra income to improve welfare, which in turn could curb excess savings, lift consumption and broaden the fiscal base even further.

The State Taxation Administration said this month that citizens declared they owed more than 160 billion yuan ($24 billion) in tax on offshore-trust income, including more than 120 billion yuan collected in October, up 90% year-on-year. The reckoning continues as tycoons negotiate with officials and their advisers on how to comply with Beijing's stepped-up enforcement in recent months to tax overseas income, including those from offshore trusts. The bigger and more durable prize is information. Beijing now has clearer visibility into the fortunes held by the top 1% of earners, who already contribute more than 50% of income taxes.

Yet the levies China collected in 2025 equated to just 12.6% of GDP; the OECD average is 34.1%, though the latter includes social-security contributions. The Chinese state’s take increases to 25% once fees and other income are counted, but it is still shrinking as a percentage of the Chinese economy.

There are plenty of places to look next. Beijing is considering ending the income-tax exemption on government-bond interest and has debated a sugar levy. Senior advisers have recently floated an inheritance tax, where there is four decades of reform-era wealth up for grabs.

This could all finance stronger welfare without further penalising formal employment. Bolstering pensions for an ageing population is one option. The International Monetary Fund proposes raising more from income, capital and property while cutting social-security contributions from employers and employees, which absorb 38.5% of labour costs compared with roughly 30% across the G20.

Such reforms are easier said than done. Introducing property and inheritance taxes have been under discussion for two decades without resolution. For now, Beijing is stressing that it’s only increasing enforcement of existing tax rules and reducing tax exemptions to be more in line with global norms. But the early success with offshore trusts may encourage authorities to go further.

Chinese taxpayers have declared more than 160 billion yuan ($24 billion) in ​taxes on offshore trust income, of which at least 120 billion yuan was paid in October, the official Xinhua news agency reported on November 12.
That would make October 2026 the biggest month of income-tax collection in China's history, Gavekal Dragonomics analysts noted in a report published on November 18.
